title: Privacy & disclosure
blurb: Re-identification, suppression and noise: what to check before a table, map or dataset goes out.

cards.prompt: Sweeney's classic re-identification finding: which three attributes uniquely identify about 87% of the US population?
cards.answer: 5-digit ZIP code, gender, and full date of birth.
cards.why: The general lesson: a handful of ordinary attributes is enough to single people out, so 'no names' is not 'anonymous'.
cards.source: L. Sweeney, Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely (2000)

cards.prompt: What is k-anonymity, and why isn't it enough to protect people by itself?
cards.answer: A dataset is k-anonymous when each record looks the same as at least k-1 others on the attributes that could identify someone, such as age, postcode and gender. It isn't enough because if everyone in such a group shares the same sensitive value, that value is revealed anyway, and because an attacker who knows something extra about a person can still narrow them down.
points: Each record is indistinguishable from at least k-1 others on identifying attributes
Fails when a whole group shares the same sensitive value
Fails against an attacker with outside knowledge
So it's one safeguard, not a guarantee

cards.prompt: You suppress one small cell in a published table but keep the row and column totals. What's the problem?
cards.answer: The hidden value can be recovered by subtracting from the totals. You need complementary (secondary) suppression of other cells, or rounding or perturbation, so that no hidden cell can be derived.
points: Recoverable by subtraction from margins
Complementary suppression
Or rounding/perturbation
cards.source: Federal Committee on Statistical Methodology, Statistical Policy Working Paper 22

cards.prompt: What does differential privacy promise, and what is the trade-off?
cards.answer: It promises that the published results would be almost the same whether or not any one person's data was included, so the results reveal very little about any individual. It works by adding carefully calibrated random noise. The trade-off is accuracy: stronger privacy means more noise, and every additional statistic released from the same data uses up some of a fixed privacy budget.
points: Results are nearly the same with or without any one person
Achieved by adding calibrated noise
More privacy means less accuracy
Each release spends from a finite privacy budget
cards.source: Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014)
cards.why: The strength of the guarantee is set by a parameter called epsilon: smaller means more private and noisier.

cards.prompt: What is the mosaic effect, and how does it change how you review a data release?
cards.answer: Releases that are each harmless can be combined, with each other or with outside data, to identify people. So you assess a release against everything already published and plausibly available, not in isolation, and you track what has gone out before.
points: Individually safe releases can combine into disclosure
Outside data counts too
Review cumulatively, not release by release
Keep a record of what has been published
cards.source: US OMB M-13-13 (Open Data Policy); disclosure-control literature

cards.prompt: Data minimization and purpose limitation: state each in one line.
cards.answer: Minimization: collect and keep only the data needed for a stated purpose. Purpose limitation: don't reuse data for purposes incompatible with the one it was collected for.
cards.why: Both appear in the Fair Information Practice Principles and in GDPR Article 5. Data you never collected can't leak.

cards.prompt: A team wants to publish a map of individual service requests at their exact addresses. What risks do you raise, and what do you propose?
cards.answer: Exact points at single-household addresses identify households, and some request types are sensitive: welfare checks, possible domestic or mental-health situations, complaints about a neighbor. The person who complained can often be inferred. Propose aggregating to a street segment, block or larger area, or snapping points to the block. Suppress small counts and exclude sensitive request types. Get legal or privacy review, and publish documentation explaining the protections.
points: Household identification at single-household addresses
Sensitive request types
Requester inference
Aggregate or snap locations; suppress small counts; exclude sensitive types
Privacy/legal review and documented protections
